I presented yesterday at an AICTE event at Acharya Institute of Graduate Studies- Bengaluru on the topic, "Uses of Generative AI in Service Industry." 

It was less about how things work, more about what Gen AI is already doing across financial services, hiring, healthcare, education and logistics: answering customers in their own language, resolving a student's doubt in real time, reading the paperwork nobody wants to read, doing reviews of complex legal contracts, etc.

Where it goes next matters more for our students. From assistants that answer, to agents that act, to orchestration, with one person supervising several agents. Alongside that, hybrid systems: a language model paired with a judgment/ decision model built for bounded decisions, each doing what it does best.
I closed with a live demonstration on staffing paperwork. Unglamorous, and exactly where the value sits. Grateful to the hosts.

Spent tonight at East Bay Founders in San Ramon. Customer Success in the AI Era. Bishop Ranch.

East Bay Founders put operators in a room. Sugata Sanyal  hosted. Ted Hulsy and Emily Valencia helped build it. Matthew Herrick sponsored it.

Melissa McMillan showed an agentic dashboard running live. Usage, friction, risk, and what needs a human next. See the book in real time instead of waiting for the QBR.

Then someone asked the simple question. Who owns the customer.

Maranda Dziekonski did not give it to CS or sales. Everyone owns the customer.

Nathan Trueblood took that into the second panel. Trust still comes from follow through, real value, and a real relationship. What changes is how you scale it. From one person, to a system, to a culture.

Kimthu Doan on hiring. Early on, customer obsession beats a polished resume.

The line I am carrying home. Customers are not signing long contracts anymore. The day the deal closes, renewal is already the job.

Activity is not value. More tickets is not better. Silence is bad. Noise is not the goal. What is the customer doing that represents value to them.

Build the agents. Then spend the time you get back on the call that actually changes the account. The one where a person stays because another person showed up.

Thank you to East Bay Founders, Sugata, Ted, Emily, Matthew Herrick, Melissa, Maranda, Vishnu, Kimthu, and Nathan. Virginia B. Hillman

Teams that invest in robust data contracts and automated quality gates are the ones that can safely accelerate their AI-augmented workflows.

Another trend that demands attention is the rise of "everyone's a workflow" thinking. The scarcity is no longer in writing SQL or Python but in designing the orchestration logic that governs how AI and human collaborators interact. The most effective teams I have observed are moving away from monolithic pipelines toward modular, event-driven workflows where each component is independently testable and replaceable. This is not just about resilience; it is about allowing AI to refactor or optimize a single step without destabilizing the entire data product.

The governance angle is also maturing. Proactive data engineering now means embedding policy into the pipeline surface, not just at the query layer. Tools that enforce data lineage, access controls, and cost attribution at the event level are becoming standard. The teams that treat governance as a reactive compliance exercise will find themselves unable to keep pace with the speed of AI-driven iterations.

AI is and isn’t the reason you can’t find a job.

The current job market is non-existent. The unemployment rate, job openings, labor participation, and other metrics are meaningless. The reality on the ground is hiring is frozen.

Recruiters have responded by being positive, encouraging, and giving well-intentioned advice. They talk about authenticity in the era of AI-enhanced resumes and cover letters, and in the end, they land on “lean into your network.”

But as a blue-collar kid who was the first in his family to attend college, the reality is most networks result from social capital that was inherited, not earned or cultivated.

Why is hiring frozen? The two-letter answer to all questions: AI.

This isn’t about AI and ATS rejecting qualified applicants, or weird AI interviews. This isn’t about the unstoppable job-killing juggernaut of AI. 

This is about AI’s total failure to replace people. Its intent was getting rid of people entirely; that has failed.

AI isn’t getting much better, it’s being asked to do less as the goal posts move from person replacement to utility. 

AI is also failing at that task because it takes productive, creative human labor and turns it into perpetual editing; mistakes that come at unsustainable prices.

C-suites driven by a combination of unhappiness that demographics shrunk the labor pool and increased wages, and FOMO driving quarterly earnings calls and stock prices, made big promises based on technology they overestimated.

The hiring freezes we’re experiencing are because AI plans to replace labor have failed. The AI contracts they’ve signed are destroying budgets and margins. Corporate boards and Wall Street have questions, and productivity has suffered. There’s work to be done and money to make. They need people, not AI.

American markets are now more concentrated than at any time in history, so there are no fears of losing market share to competitors and companies have decided to make less rather than pay more.

So instead of accepting reality, we get:

- Ghost jobs intended to signal growth to Wall Street and measure the talent pool.

- Recruiters inquiring about your rate just to gauge the market for jobs that don’t exist.

- Inflated applicant numbers from listings posted and reposted. 

- Companies asserting they can’t find people with the requisite skills (even though transferable skills are not a new concept).

None of this is true.

Don’t believe those who only have advice that places blame entirely on job seekers. You aren’t responsible for AI hype, C-suite euphoria about AI freeing it from labor market reality, a lack of skills, your age, or anything else.

It all lands right where this began.
